I want to be able to be free, and with Tepperware, even though if I would have the party dated for, like, tonight, and my husband comes home and says, gee, let's go so-and-so tonight, I can call up one of the other Tepperware dealers, and she'll do the party for me, and I get commission off of it, and I don't have to stay home because I have to work. That's kind of like a pretty good deal. It is. Well, there's a couple, three other Tepperware dealers here in town, so we all kind of work together, you know, if one's sick and can't do their party, or something comes up, so then we just give one of the other girls a call, and they go do it for us. Do you sell Tepperware for your own enjoyment, or is it just so that you can have a few extra things, or is it just to add money to the family account? Well, it's kind of a rule of all, really. I went into it mainly because I was bored sitting at home, and I had a girlfriend that has three little ones, and she was always coming over, and she was going to go somewhere for five minutes, and would I watch the children, and mine were all in school, and I'd end up sitting home all day long watching her children, so this way with Tepperware I have something I have to go do, so I don't have to go for it. I like babies till they start to crawl, and somebody else can take them to their teens. I'd have been better off if I went to work at the pediatrics nurse. What do you foresee as the future for your children? I don't know. I just, I mean, more jobs, more education, jobs. Do you have any expectations? Well, I'm hoping they all get a chance to go to college, because I feel like now college is as important as high school was when I went to school, and they just really have to have it to even get along in the world, I think, and job wise, just so that's something they enjoy doing, because it's really too bad when people have to work at jobs that they don't like, and they keep going to work every morning. Do you want to go to college, Mary Ann?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I'd be glad. I want to become a nurse, not a lab technician.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Have you ever thought about being a doctor?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, not really. A lab technician brings in more money than you can sit there and experiment and stuff.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She started out wanting to be a nurse, and then we started explaining to her the difference between being a nurse and if she would be a lab technician. I mean, there really is a lot more opportunities in being a technician than there is a nurse. Do you belong to any organizations at school that are investigating all the possibilities? She's just going up to the high school this year to where she'll just be starting into having this type of thing. Last year she was in ninth grade, which is at the junior high, and I think this year she'll probably be able to join future nurses, which I belong to, or some of these other type things where they can get into it a little more deeply. Did you ever consider later going back and taking courses so that you could become a nurse? I had really thought seriously about it when I was in Coeur d'Alene, and they were just starting this LPN course down at the college, and now of course they have the full RN course down there now, but I had thought about when I got the children up and could afford it and so on that I would enjoy going back to school and maybe becoming a nurse. Of course at that time my thinking was more towards being the LPN and then maybe later going into Spokane and being an RN, but now they've got the RN course at North Idaho College too. Are you still considering that? I don't think so anymore. This was before I got remarried, and Martin and I just rather be able to just, when we get the kids grown, this idea of life is two big motorcycles and stop when we're hungry and work long enough to have a meal and just take off cross-country. We're going to have our childhood after we get the kids grown up. Have you ever thought about having a child of your own together? No way. Three's enough. It really is financially hard to raise three, and then he has a boy of his own, so. And they're kind of, he's kind of like I am, he, you know. We love the kids we got, but we don't want any more. If I had to do every game, I probably wouldn't have, I wouldn't have had as many as I did have. Well, three isn't really that many. I know, but there's so many things. I mean, now Mary Ann, she's old enough that we can take her with us now, like even with the motorcycles. As soon as she gets her driver's license, she can go with us. But the other two we've got to find a babysitter for. Of course, now once we get her with the license, then we put each of the boys on behind us and go. But before we had three kids, there was no way we could take all the bikes out on the road because with no license for the kids, they can't ride on the roads. So, and there's so many things that he wants to do that, you know, or that we'd like to do that we can't because of the children holding us back. Where did you learn about childbirth and child raising? I assume you had your children at the hospital. Mm-hmm. I don't remember if I went to those prenatal courses before I had CIS or not. No, I, yeah, I did because I had it with no, at Coeur d'Alene at the courthouse, they'd have prenatal classes to where you went and they taught you the basics of the natural childbirth. And so I had learned from that, you know. And then, of course, being interested in nursing, I'd read quite a few books, not technical books, but, you know, books on childbirth and so on. So I had learned from that. And then, of course, at the time, I was real interested in children. Like I said, I'd wanted to be a pediatrics nurse, so. Between running the nursing and the children and so on, I'd read quite a bit about it. Did you have all of your children natural childbirths?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm scared of a needle. That was easier to put up with childbirth pains than it was to put up with all that needle coming at me. Was it a good experience for you having the children? Mm-hmm. I mean, did it feel good physically? As far as the pain and so on, it wasn't that bad. I would have a dozen more as far as the childbirth and so on. It just wasn't any problem at all. I didn't have any problems having my children. I was in labor a long time with her, but there wasn't to the point that it was anything that was upsetting or anything. I've talked to just a few women who said it was really a beautiful experience. Mm-hmm. One of them said she would almost right then, she was ready to have another child because of that, but that they only wanted two, so she didn't do it. Yeah. Yeah, it's not really that bad. I mean, I think a lot of the problem is the fact that going into it's scary to start with, and I really feel that the natural childbirth courses are well worth anybody's time to go to because you can learn to diminish the childbirth pain if you know how to react to it properly. I mean, when you're scared, you're tense, and when you're tense, it hurts worse. I mean, it's that way with a shot or anything else. You just, if you can learn to relax and convince yourself that this isn't going to hurt, it's not going to hurt as bad as if you're scared, oh, it's going to kill me, you know. And I really think that even though there's complications, they do need to have maybe possibly some type of a pain reliever of some kind that's still in all, if they know what's going on and are prepared for it to an extent it's not as bad as when they go into it just cold turkey. Okay, let's go back a little bit. What types of occupations did the other two husbands have? They both worked in sawmills. I want to find out something about your reaction to being a minor's wife. Had you ever thought about being a minor's wife? Were you ever concerned about the danger steps? When I married Martin, he wasn't working underground. He was working in the sink plant, and then the chance came up for the big to go underground. Of course, this was after the Sunshine disaster up here. And I just didn't even have any qualms about him going underground because I mean with all the years that have been mines up here, there just is not that many accidents. This is the only disaster that we've had. And as far as I'm concerned, it's just a one in a million thing. I mean it's more dangerous I think driving on the highway than it is working underground in the mine. Have they changed a lot of the safety precautions since then? Now, see here works for Bunker Hill, which is a completely different mine than Sunshine. And Bunker Hill, as I understood it, I mean I wasn't here at the time and I knew nothing of it. The designers at Bunker Hill's safety precautions are different than Sunshine. And of course each mill company is different. It doesn't make any difference if it's a sawmill or a truck. And he says they take as much precaution as what they possibly can and still be able to work. I mean, you know, he loves it underground. He wouldn't go back to working in the sink plants or anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh really?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh. He was only down there a couple weeks and he could have went back, you know, within a certain length of time. And I think his first week he was like, boy, you're not going to catch me back in that sink plant. He likes it underground. Yeah, and of course, I mean, if I were to work under there, he says I wouldn't feel that way, but I get claustrophobia and I just know that if I went underground I'd just climb a wall. I've never been underground, but the idea of being confined in bothers me. But he says that the rooms are real big and you don't feel like you're underground or confined down there, so he likes it. What is it about being underground that he likes so much? I don't know what it is. He enjoys his job down there. He really likes it. Before he became a miner, he was working tearing the timber down in a skip tender, I think it's called. Anyhow, it's kind of like an elevator thing, but they take the lumber down to the miners. This is what he did until he got a chance to become a miner. And even that he enjoyed. He liked being under there. And he enjoys his job and this is what's important. I'd rather have him happy with his job and maybe there is more danger down there, but as far as I'm concerned, he's happy, so that's the difference, you know. Are you concerned about the types of pollution that they talk about in Kellogg's? No, because my aunt and uncle lived in Widener years and years ago, and at that time it was so much worse. And I really think that they're really doing what they can to try to clean it up. There's some days it's bad, but there's other days that, you know, a few days back they had a real bad day, I guess, but I was gone, so I didn't really notice it. But I think a lot of it's, they need the precautions, yes, but I think they're going overboard on trying to get them put through. I mean, some of the people I think are really fanatical about it. I don't think it needs to be quite that drastic. Have you taken precautions around the house to keep down on the lead? No. I mean, I keep my house clean, you know, but I mean, I don't try to, I don't worry about it. And I've always seen kids wash their hands before they eat and so on, even when we lived at Caden Lake. So, you know, I think this is where a lot of them are getting it, because you do see little grubby kids around putting their dirty hands in their mouth and so on. I think this could be one of the factors, not that their mothers are dirty or anything, but just kids are that way, and my children are all big enough that they look past that stage when I moved up here. In fact, my kids hadn't even been tested for lead until just the other day. And when they come around door to door and they got my little one, the two other ones are too old to be tested, but they did test the little one. But I won't care for a while, I'll really put on it. That's nice. How long has he lived here, or how long have you lived here? Just two years, maybe two years in December that we moved up here. It would be interesting to see how this compares with people with little children who have been here all their lives. I've got friends that have lived here all their lives, I mean they were grown adults, you know, and they just haven't done anything that drastic has. Yeah, I mean I think that's just a little... You're alone? Just a minute. Why? I can tell she's worried about getting her life. I just assumed she was. Let me see, let me think for a minute, some of the other things that we usually ask about. A lot of the questions that we ask are about the depression and things like that, but that one has affected your life. Did the war affect your life in any way? Not that I can really think of, because I was just a year old when Pearl Harbor was bombed, and then my father got... Mom had to sign for him to go into the service, he went into the service, and he was probably 30 I think when he went into the Army. I'm not sure if he went in after Pearl Harbor or not, but anyhow, when the war broke out, my father did enlist, and he was in the service, and other than that I really can't... Was he overseas? No, he wasn't. He was due to go overseas, and the day that his former squadron was to pull out, something come through that they didn't have to leave, so he was in the states all the time. Was he away from home? Yes, he was. Did that affect your life in any way that you remember? No, because I was so little I didn't remember any of it until after about... I think it was about seven that I first remember, and of course he was home by then, and it didn't bother me, and my mother had murder and rumors in the house while dad was gone, so... What about the three of them? No, none of my family was... I mean we realized it was going on and so on, and us kids had always been raised that... My brother was expected to, when he got called by the draft, he was expected to go in the service, I mean that's what it was, but he did volunteer for the Navy, and he's been in the Navy now for nine years, and this is the way I feel about my boys, I mean if there was some kind of a national emergency before they needed, I mean in the services and mine are old enough to go, I would be very unhappy and probably practically disown them if they ran to Canada to hide or something, because I mean if they're going to live here they have to fight for it too if it's necessary. How did you feel about the Vietnamese war? I think that we could have done a lot more than what we did, I think we just were sitting back and waiting, I feel that if we would have went in there and done a little more, that maybe we could have changed the way that it went, I didn't like the idea of sitting there as advisors and our men getting shot up, and more or less not even fighting back. You would have just gone in there and done something and gotten out, rather than sticking around and not doing much. Right. This is the way I feel about it, I mean, of course I wasn't there, and you hear so many different things, you know, one way or the other, to where you just are not sure, but I think either we shouldn't have sat there at all, or else we should have went in and done something and gotten out, one of the two. Did your parents expect for you to go on to school? I think they would have liked to, but being a child while I was pregnant I couldn't, so that was... And they had, I think, really, they had wanted me to adopt her out, so that I could go on, but I wanted to keep my baby, so it was a squabble over keeping her more than a squabble over going to school. Was there, aside from your parents, how was the reaction of your friends toward you being pregnant? Yeah. Hmm. I didn't have a whole lot of friends, and a few close friends I had, just, you know, I mean, it wasn't taken for granted as much as it is now, but they just kind of took that too well, and anybody can make a mistake, and they just kind of go back to it, I guess. Did you know very much about birth control at the time? No. Very little? Yeah, it was just, I don't know, they even said they had to peel off since that time, so. Okay. I probably was taken as a kid, so, but I really didn't know that much about it, really. You don't have to answer this, okay? If the same thing were to happen to your daughter, would you want her to get married, or would you be willing for her to just keep her child without getting married? That didn't even really do that much good as far as I was concerned to get married, as far as I was concerned, just a waste of time and effort, because what Mom and Dad wanted accomplished had been undone anyhow, so. And like I said, now there isn't the stigmatism, I don't think, on it, but there was at the time when I was pregnant, and I hope she doesn't get pregnant before she gets married, but if she does, it's her decision whether she wants to get married, and it's her decision whether she wants to keep her baby or not.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you make family decisions? How do you make decisions that involve your children?

words: Usually just whoever's around, depending on what it is, of course, but whoever's around makes the decision as to whether they can go or do something or whatever, or if it's something really drastic, then my husband and I talk it over, and he usually gets his way.

words: In family decisions, do your children take a part?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Sometimes, not too often. Usually it's my husband's and my decision, but sometimes we, no, depends on what it is.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: If your husband were considering taking another job and moving, who would have influence in that sort of decision?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: If he wanted to take another job and move, we would move.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You would just go?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'd go.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have any qualms about moving to California? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We were living in Port Lane for a while, and at the time he was working the changing shifts and pulling a lot of doubles for you.

words: Make sure it fits with my question.

words: Do you have a garden here? No.

words: Did you have a garden in Port Lane? Mm-hmm.

words: Last year we planted a few things, but they didn't do much. I was too busy doing other things to take care of the garden.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The garden isn't a priority then? No. Have you ever canned food or frozen food or anything like that? Oh, yeah.

words: Until the last couple years, I canned every year. Especially the green beans, because I lived over where they grew them. I didn't have to bother picking them. words: Do you enjoy canning?

words: Yeah, I do. It's a lot of work, but when you look at those shelves that are all full, you can see what you've done anyhow, where housework you don't. That's true.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It doesn't seem to get un- That's true. It doesn't seem to get un-done.

words: Quite as bad as that housework.

words: I never really thought about that.

words: It's kind of like making bread or anything else, where you've got something that you can see it, that you accomplished, etc. When the ironing's all done, it's all put in the closet. Nobody sees it. But when you've got your canning all done, you can go down and brag for a year about what you did on canning.

words: Do you bake your own bread?

words: I did for a while. I take spurts. I go on a spurt and I'll bake bread for quite a while. Then I'll get off on another tangent and do something else for a while.

words: What other type of tangents do you get off on?

words: Knitting or painting. Now it's selling Tupperware.

words: What type of painting do you do?

words: It's yard text and tri-can paints, where you paint pillowcases or tablecloths or pictures or whatever.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's pretty nice.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's the only type of painting I have. I can't tell if that or painting the outside of the barn, because as an artist I am not.

words: Do you work on the motorcycle as far as anything mechanically?

I'm mechanically inclined, but I've never had enough practice to know what I'm doing for sure.

words: Would you like to learn more about that?

words: I wouldn't mind learning mechanics. When I was in high school, my highest aptitude was in mechanics. Of course at that time I was very upset about it, because I wanted to be a nurse. words: Did they have any mechanics courses, or were you interested in taking them when you were in high school or anything like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't think there was any mechanics courses. There was woodworking for the boys and that type of stuff, but there wasn't mechanics. And like I said, at that time I was really upset, because I had shown mechanical abilities. The counselor told me I'd be a good mechanic, and at the time I wanted to be a nurse. He says, well, it has advantages even in that, because your nurses that work with you, people that are in the iron lungs or on some of these machines, have to know mechanics to an extent to be able to get the machine working right away, in case it should stop. The patient needs to have their machine, so. I hadn't really thought of it on that terms, but...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there anything that you've ever really wanted to do that you've been toward it,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: because you were a woman? Not really. I am kind of anti-women's lib to an extent. I mean, I really feel that women's lib had a purpose when it started out, but I think some of it's getting carried a little too far. For instance, when a woman is doing the same type of job as a man, definitely they should get the same pay, but I don't think they should squawk and try to get every job that every man has. I mean, just like up here at Bunker Hill, there's lots and lots of the girls that go up there and work, and now they're wanting down in the mine where there's no facilities down in the mine for the women to be working alongside of the men. And a lot of the guys at first used to help the girls that come up to Bunker Hill, like at the zinc plant, and help them and so on, where now they're kind of the girls that got to do it on their own. And I don't think a woman should have a job that pays the same as a man if she can't do the whole job. If she has to holler for somebody else to come help her do her share of the job, she shouldn't have it. Do they holler now, or are they really doing it on their own? I really don't know how it is now, because like I said, my husband is underground where they don't have the women, but there for a while they used to kind of halfway expect the guys, you know, if the wheelbarrow's too heavy, the guy will come help me or whatever, you know. The guys have kind of gotten away from it now, and I don't know just how much the girls are doing now, or if they're able to do their full jobs or not. When you say facilities underground, are you talking about a restroom sort of thing? Are there any facilities for the men? Well, there's places where there is a restroom type thing, you know, but most of the time they just, as long as it's urinating, it's just in the ditches. They just don't even bother. There's ditches with water running through them, they use those. So it doesn't matter as long as there's just men there, but if there were women there it would complicate things. Right. What are the other things about women's slips that you're addicted to? I just think they're making too big of a deal of it. I mean, like I said, I do feel that when they started out that they had a legitimate right, because there were women that were doing the same type of job as men. They were getting all those paid because they were a woman instead of getting the same pay rate as a man. But they're carrying it to such an extreme now that no matter what you're doing or what kind of thing it is the men have the attitude, well, she's a woman, let her do it herself. I mean, they're all taking the opinion that all of the women want women's lib. And personally I like a man to open a door for me or if the couch is too heavy to move I holler for him to come help me. I mean, I can't see busting my back when I can get a man to help me do it. Change a tire? I can change a car tire, but if some man comes along I'm going to play helpless and get him to change it for me. And they're ruining a lot of this because, I mean, now they use a whole lot of do it herself. And where it used to be anytime a woman was stuck alongside the road a man would always stop and help her. And now lots of times I've been out on the freeway in the rain changing a tire and nobody would stop to help her. This is one of the reasons for my Tupperware is because it gives me a few hours away from the kids and so on. And yet I've got one girlfriend that she's got two children of her own. She babysits children all the time and she's just as good as can be. And I would be pulling my hair out if I had to put up with kids all the time. And I think sometimes they get better care and more attention from mothers when mothers have been away for a while. Is that what happens with you? Yeah. I don't go ranting and raving and screaming quite as much. And we're able to have more things and do more things with the children because I do have a little extra money. I mean, like, lots and lots of evenings she walks us to the park or out chasing around the countryside with Linda doing something. Some of the time we have Linda with us. Second mother to us. Yeah. She wraps Martin around her finger. Don't ya? She wraps Martin around her finger, doesn't she? When she wants to do something and I don't let her, she goes sees Martin. That's how you'll finally get your driver's license, right? No, they both agreed on that. Are you glad you had driver's training? Yeah.
